clips.title: The Bus Factor: How Many People Can You Lose Before Everything Breaks?
clips.why: A short, drawn explanation of the bus factor, with real cases of projects that depended on one person, and how teams raise the number.
look: What the bus factor measures, and why one is so common.
The real cases: a whole stack resting on one maintainer, and what that made possible.
Why the number creeps down without anyone deciding it, and the ways to raise it.
clips.after: Byte, FCP Lab, Vanil and n8n each have a bus factor of one today; the handover raises it to two, and the shipped change proves it.

clips.title: Runbooks Explained: Stop Panicking When Alerts Fire
clips.why: What a runbook is and what every runbook needs, starting from the same 3 a.m. problem as our Friday night.
look: The 3 a.m. problem: the person on call did not build the thing that broke.
Why a runbook is written for that person, in the order they will use it.
Compare the parts he lists with our three: first look, symptoms, escalate.
clips.after: Each when-it-breaks page is a runbook like this, written by the builder from real failures and corrected by the second maintainer after their first real change.

clips.title: How to auto-backup n8n workflows to GitHub
clips.why: The nightly backup from our plan, built in the n8n editor: read every workflow with the n8n node, write each one to GitHub, then restore one.
look: The n8n node that lists every workflow, the same Workflows: Get many step as our plan.
How each workflow becomes one file in the repo, like the lab's backup folder.
The restore at the end: the step that turns a copy into a backup.
clips.after: Our backup has the same shape, with a token that can write to the Vanil repo only, and it only counts once a restore into a fresh n8n works.

practice.q: Vanil's workflows exist only inside n8n's database, and the database keeps 14 days of snapshots. Why add a nightly export to git as well?

options.text: A snapshot is the whole database: you cannot read, review or restore one workflow from it on its own
options.why: The export gives a readable file per workflow, with history, that a second person can review and restore one at a time.

options.text: Snapshots also store the credentials' secrets, so they must be deleted
options.why: The snapshots stay; they are the only place the credentials survive. The export adds a readable copy next to them.

options.text: Agents read n8n's database directly, and git is faster
options.why: No agent reads n8n's database. The export is for people: a second maintainer and a restore.

practice.q: In a workflow export, a node that uses a proper n8n credential carries only two fields for it. One is the name; what is the other?
practice.hint: The field a restore uses to find the credential again.
practice.why: The export points at the credential by id and name, and the secret stays in n8n's database. That is why a restore into a fresh n8n has to create the credential again.

practice.q: Put the steps of a backup that you can trust in order.
items: Export every workflow from n8n, one file each
Push them to the private Vanil repo only when the scan is clean
Start a fresh n8n that has never seen the workflows
Import the backup into it and check that every workflow is listed
practice.why: The scan comes before the push because git history is hard to clean, and the restore comes into a fresh n8n because only there can the test fail.

practice.q: Byte's page ends with: Byte is advisory; while it is down, PRs still merge with 1 approval. Why does that line matter at 22:00?

options.text: It tells the person on call how urgent the failure really is: nothing is blocked, so it can wait for a careful fix
options.why: The escalate part says what the failure costs, so a stranger does not wake people up or take risky shortcuts for a tool that blocks nothing.

options.text: It tells them to merge all open PRs while Byte is down
options.why: It describes what still works, not an order. Normal review still applies to every PR.

options.text: It tells them to switch Byte off for good
options.why: Advisory means Byte does not block merges, not that it is unimportant. The page leads to a fix, not a shutdown.

practice.q: After the walkthrough, the second maintainer must ship one small change to Byte. Who drives the change?

options.text: Byte's builder, so the change is done right
options.why: Then the second maintainer only watches again, and the handover proves nothing.

options.text: The second maintainer, with the builder only reviewing
options.why: Building, testing, deploying and fixing the page alone is the proof that a second person can keep Byte running.

options.text: Nova, so the change is fast
options.why: The point is a second person who can fix Byte at night, not one more pull request.
